accuracy.evidence: Checked against the UNCRC text: adopted by the UN in 1989, 54 articles of which 42 set out rights, covering everyone under 18. Article 12 (being heard), Article 19 (protection from harm), Article 28 (free primary education), Article 24 (health) and Article 18 (parents' primary responsibility) are cited where used. Duty bearers follow UNICEF UK RRSA wording: governments and adults working for the state, with parents and carers.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the beliefs PSHE teachers meet in KS2: rights must be earned or can be taken away as a punishment (Jake step and earned prediction), rights are the same as wants (sort deck with trainers, phone and screen time), my right beats yours (clash balance), and children must do responsibilities in exchange for rights, which UNICEF UK's guidance warns against because rights are unconditional.

lab_distinct.evidence: The flagrights lab is built on rights reasoning rather than any shared template: a swipe-sort deck of needs versus wants, a mirror that copies a child's choice onto Everyone else, a shield showing which punishments may never remove a right, a tilting balance scale for clashing rights, and duty-bearer lanes for the government, parents and children. Highest shingle overlap with any other lab is 4.8% (flag_voice).

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step makes the learner act out one core idea: sorting six cards separates rights from wants, the mirror shows a right only works if everyone else has it too, the Jake shield separates privileges like golden time from rights like food and being heard, the scale only levels when a fix keeps both rights, and the lanes assign who must make each right happen.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions are locked before the matching action: whether a phone is a right every child needs, what the right to be listened to means for other people, and whether breaking a rule means a child loses the right to be safe. Each later done message names the prediction back, for example You predicted Yes, rights have to be earned; now you know why it's No.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The Challenge rotates five questions with shuffled options, and every wrong option has its own why message: trainers are a want, always getting your way ignores other people's rights, a punishment can remove a privilege but never a right, and the duty to provide school sits with the government. Feedback is spoken through the live region and shown under the question.

readability.evidence: Kid explanation reads at Flesch-Kincaid grade 2.0 and the adult text at grade 7.0, inside the learner targets of 6.5 and 9.5. Lab prompts are one short sentence each, such as Drag the card to Right or Want, or tap a box, and key terms (right, want, privilege, duty bearer) are introduced one at a time.

no_filler.evidence: No praise padding or vague phrases: every paragraph carries a fact or rule, such as rights cannot be earned or removed, a privilege like golden time can be lost, and adults and governments are duty bearers. Explanation overlap with other lessons is 0.2% at most (Everyday kindness and care), so nothing is copied from nearby P&S lessons.

mobile.evidence: Walked on iPhone 13 and desktop: cards, mirror choices, Jake rows, balance pans and duty lanes all fit the width after pan positions were clamped inside the canvas on narrow screens. All targets are tap-or-drag with large pads below the canvas, and Show me finishes every task inside the time limit.

accessibility.evidence: axe-core reports no violations in light and dark themes on phone and desktop. Every canvas action has a button twin in the pads group with an aria-label, feedback goes to a polite status region, the emoji-only shield glyph was removed, and colours come from the theme palette so contrast holds in both themes.

sources: UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989), Articles 2, 12, 18, 19, 24 and 28
UNICEF UK Rights Respecting Schools Award: glossary (rights holders, duty bearers; rights are universal, unconditional, inherent, inalienable)
UNICEF UK Rights Respecting Schools guidance on rights and responsibilities (rights are not conditional on responsibilities)
PSHE Association Programme of Study KS1-2: Living in the wider world, L1-L3 rights, rules and responsibilities
